Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.

L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference

to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-

sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.

formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome

oral-bioavailability outcome.

records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: The query is a permanently charged quaternary pyridinium carbamate (pyridostigmine-like); the closest carbamate context physostigmine reports poor oral bioavailability, supporting F below 20%.
A charged polar small-molecule context BMS-187745 had absolute oral bioavailability 2.6% in humans, showing permanent charge can drive F well below 20%.

Multiple transferable low-F contexts remain below 20%: tilidine 3-7.6%, agomelatine under 5%, apocynin <10% in humans and 2.8-8.3% in rats, aniracetam extremely low in humans and 8.6-11.4% in rats, acamprosate about 11%, and methyl parathion <1.7% in one human case.

L5 neostigmine records show low intestinal uptake in rat jejunal loops (5.5-12.8% absorbed in 2 h) and 6.6% of dose trapped in gut wall after 3 h, providing mechanistic evidence for presystemic loss in a close quaternary carbamate analog.
C59 shows neostigmine is a P-gp substrate but with limited efflux, so efflux is not the dominant barrier; low absorption and gut-wall trapping remain the main presystemic loss mechanisms.

C21 and C24 are the only near/above-threshold values (methyl parathion about 20% in rats; tilidine one-third systemically available), but they are species- or context-specific and do not outweigh the direct low values and the query's permanent charge.

evidence_gaps: No direct oral bioavailability measurement exists for the query molecule.
No human PK or absolute F data for pyridostigmine are supplied.
Neostigmine is a close analog but not the query; rat jejunal loop absorption is not equivalent to human F.
Query hepatic clearance and carbamate hydrolysis remain uncharacterized; L6 records are for unrelated molecules (phenacetin, metoprolol, M02-M04).
Salt form and counterion are unknown.
The property tool reports neutral fraction 1 despite the formal positive charge, adding uncertainty.
